Outcome_variable.evidence_source: CSI scores were initially analyzed using the correlated growth model. The common fate growth model was estimated so that instead of each individual having one intercept and slope, each couple has one intercept and slope. Unlike the correlated growth model, the common fate growth model fit the data very well, \chi^2(6) = 2.31, p = .89; TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .00, 90%... The close fit of the model to the data suggests that relationship satisfaction follows a dyadic rather than individual pattern of growth. The nonnested nature of the Correlated Growth and Common Fate Growth models precluded the use of the traditional likelihood ratio test to evaluate differences in model fit. However, the Akaike information criterion (AIC) and sample size—adjusted Bayesian information criterion (BIC) can still be used to compare models, with smaller values indicating better fit (Bentler & Chou, 1987). The AIC for the correlated growth model is 88.79, and the sample-size adjusted BIC is 100.34. The common fate growth model resulted in a AIC is 50.31 and a sample-size adjusted BIC of 64.17, both indicating that the common fate growth model provided superior fit to the data.4 Table 3 shows the model parameters of the common fate growth model. Estimates of the slope reveal that there is a significant decline in couple's relationship satisfaction. Estimates of the variance for the intercepts and slopes also reveal significant heterogeneity among couples for both initial levels of relationship satisfaction and couple-level change. Individuallevel covariation in relationship satisfaction is present in significant autocovariances across all three time points. The positive sign of the autocovariances suggests that individuals were more similar across time than a purely dyadic growth pattern could account for. The nonsignificant covariance between the intercept and slope indicates that initial dyadic levels of relationship satisfaction are unrelated to changes in relationship satisfaction. The results of the two models of dyadic change in relationship satisfaction indicate that the common fate growth model outperforms the correlated growth model in describing how relationship satisfaction changes in married couples.
